title: Family discharge planning meetings and 30-day readmission in adults aged 75 and over
subtitle: Design not yet settled: exposure is recorded in notes, and meetings are chosen for complex families
statement: Hospital social workers hold family discharge planning meetings for some patients aged 75 and over with complicated discharges, and the hospital is considering making them standard to avoid readmission penalties. It is not known locally whether a meeting that the family attends and that ends with a written plan is associated with fewer readmissions within 30 days once the greater complexity of patients chosen for meetings is taken into account. Whether the family attended is recorded only in the social work notes.
whoAffected: Patients aged 75 and over with complicated discharges, their families and carers, the social work team whose time is at stake, and the ward teams who organise discharge.
whatHurts: Early readmission is distressing for older patients and carers, costs the hospital a penalty, and may reflect a plan that did not work at home. Making meetings standard without evidence would take social work time from other patients, while dropping them could remove support that matters to families.
currentPractice: Meetings are booked at the discretion of the social worker, more often for complicated families; attendance and plans are written in free-text notes; readmissions are counted monthly without any link to social work activity.
whyNow: The medical director wants a recommendation before the budget round in May 2027, and senior social worker time for reading notes is available this winter.
constraints: About 120 hours of senior social worker time for reading notes between November 2026 and February 2027; no contact with patients or families; an answer is needed before the hospital's budget round in May 2027.
patientCenteredGoal: Older patients go home with a plan their family understands and can carry out, and avoid readmissions that a better plan could prevent.
summary: Problem framed; the design family is left unresolved because the fair comparison depends on how exposure can be measured and how complexity drives selection.
